Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Bear Shea, and I am here today representing the Department of Education speaking in support of L.D. #98, An Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine
Program, which seeks to add school counselor as a postbaccalaureate certification that is eligible for financial assistance under the Educators for Maine Program administered by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME).
This bill would expand educator positions for participating in postsecondary credentialling at a
time when incentives for joining the field of education are an important recruitment strategy.
Educators for Maine is a competitive, merit-based, forgivable loan for Maine students pursuing careers in education, speech pathology, or childcare. These students plan to live and work in Maine after their graduation. During their coursework, students must maintain a 3.0 grade point
average and must be pursuing their initial certification. As of today, teachers, speech language
pathologists, and childcare providers are the only allowable certifications for this program.
In 2023, the Maine Department of Education received a five-year, $9 million grant through the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, to increase school-based mental health staff and services in Maine. Expanding Access in School Enviromnents (EASE) Maine has provided grants to nine high-need school administrative units (SAUs) to support their efforts to recruit and retain mental health providers and expand services to students.
Funds from the EASE Maine grant, which is managed by the Department's Office of School and
Student Supports, would be used to augment FAME funding in order to support the school
mental health professional pipeline. The funding is estimated to support approximately two years
of FAME awards. Cmrently, school counselors are not eligible to access any FAME programs. Other school based mental health professionals can access FAME programs through the medical professionals` programs, and teachers and speech pathologists can access FAME educator
programs.
For these reasons, the Department of Education is in support of L.D. 98, An Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine Program. I am happy to answer any questions the
Committee may have, and I will be available for Work sessions on this bill.

Testimony in Support of LD 98
An Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine Program
Senator Rafferty, Representative Brennan, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, as a former counselor educator and certified school counselor in Maine, I strongly support LD 98, which seeks to expand the Educators for Maine Program to include school counselors as eligible positions.
School Counselors are educators. They are certified by the Maine Department of Education just like teachers are. They serve all students in the school, as the role defines. They provide an important service to schools supporting the academic, career, and social emotional needs of all students in Pk-12 to help them achieve success in school and make plans for their future.
To earn a 075 School Counselor certificate in Maine, one must have a bachelors degree and a master's degree. Today's master's degrees in School Counseling most often require 60 credits of coursework, a significant investment on the part of the student. As a counselor educator I saw many wonderful school counseling students struggle with debt from student loans.
As I am sure you are aware, there is a serious shortage of school counselors in Maine. Ensuring that school counseling students can apply for the Educators for Maine program is one significant and fiscally responsible way to address this workforce shortage.
I urge you to support LD 98 132. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Deborah L. Drew, Ed.D., LCPC, 075 School Counselor

Testimony in Support of LD 98 An Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine Program
Senator Rafferty, Representative Brennan, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, on behalf of the Maine School Counselor Association (MESCA), which supports the success of all students by empowering, uniting, and advocating for Maine School Counselors, we are submitting this testimony in strong support of LD 98, which seeks to expand the Educators for Maine Program to include school counselors as eligible positions.
Maine faces a growing shortage of school counselors, particularly in rural and underserved communities. School counselors play a critical role in fostering student success, addressing mental health challenges, ensuring career and college readiness, and fostering a connection between home and school. Often, they are the sole provider of these services in their communities. The need for well-trained, accredited professionals is at an all-time high, and this bill provides an effective mechanism to attract and retain qualified individuals in these essential roles.
School counselors align directly with the goals of LD 98, which prioritizes supporting education professionals in areas with the greatest need. By incentivizing individuals to pursue school counseling, Maine can work toward addressing gaps in student support services, ensuring every child has access to the support and mental health resources they deserve.
Including school counselors in the Educators for Maine Program is both fiscally viable and necessary. The Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) currently administers this program, and expanding the eligibility criteria to include school counselors would be a seamless addition. A person does not casually go into the field of school counseling; the field has grown and evolved over the years, now requiring a master's degree with 60 credit hours, a 600-hour internship (often unpaid), and practicum experience, which leads to a hefty price tag for individuals looking to support students and provide them the opportunities for success in Maine.
For these reasons, I urge you to support LD 98 132 to strengthen Maine's educational workforce and provide necessary assistance to those committed to serving our students. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Rebecca Edelman PhD, MESCA Board Chair (chair@maineschoolcounselor.org) Scott Harris EdS, MESCA Past Board Chair

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs: The University of Maine System (UMS) is the state's leading provider of certified school counselors.
Current State school counselor certification requires an individual to have attained a master's or doctoral degree in counseling through an accredited program approved to prepare school counselors or that offers aligned coursework. Through the University of Southern Maine (USM), our System provides the only such public program in the state with 60 graduate students currently pursuing a Master of Science in Counseling degree with a concentration in School Counseling.
USM's program is nationally accredited, informed by its close connections to the field and through an advisory board, and has a strong record of preparing graduates for school counseling employment and success. More than half of its students attain the State's conditional school counseling certification and work as full-time school counselors during their field placement experiences, and almost all students secure employment in Maine schools before graduation.
Through this program and our Systemwide partnerships with Maine's PK-12 districts, UMS is acutely aware of the critical need for highly qualified counselors in our state's schools -- especially in rural regions. Even though USM's program is the state's most affordable -- costing about 40% less per credit hour for in-state students than the private option, we believe that extending some form of financial assistance to aspiring school counselors, whether through scholarships or loan forgiveness, would make the required advanced degree more accessible. Doing so would likely result in more people pursuing school counseling careers instead of private practice and help address these severe shortages for the benefit of Maine students, families, schools and communities.
Our System is also the State's leading provider of classroom-ready teachers, having awarded nearly 4,000 education degrees or certificates in the past five years. The FAME-administered Educators for Maine program has been an essential resource for recruiting students into our educator preparation programs and then retaining them to work in our state's schools or childcare settings after graduation.

We know the existing funding for Educators for Maine is not meeting demand and are sensitive to putting further pressure on the program. Having highly qualified school counselors in a district directly supports student success by providing essential academic, social-emotional, and career guidance, ensuring students receive the interventions and resources they need to thrive. Counselors also play a vital role in connecting families with community resources that reduce barriers to learning, such as mental health services, food assistance, and housing support. Additionally, they collaborate with teachers, administrators, and community partners to create a support network for students, reducing the burdens on school staff and mitigating burnout. Valerie Caruso Augusta LD 98
Valerie Caruso
I am a professional educator for over 30 years specializing in special education systems.The percentage of Maine students identified as having an educational disability is higher than the national average-over 19%. As of January 2022, there were 32,641 students enrolled in Maine public schools with an identified disability and an individualized education plan, or 19.5% of all students. This was 650 more special education students than in January 2020, when there were 31,991 students with identified disabilities. Special education plays a crucial role in ensuring that all students, regardless of their abilities or disabilities, have the opportunity to succeed in the educational system. However, for many schools, the resources allocated to special education programs are insufficient to meet the diverse needs of students with disabilities. It is my firm belief that special education funding should be increased. Doing so would not only help provide the necessary resources for these students but also promote a more inclusive and equitable education system for everyone.
Despite the growing recognition of the importance of special education, many schools still face significant funding shortfalls in this area. Special education students often require individualized instruction, specialized staff, and tailored resources--such as assistive technologies, therapies, and behavior management programs. Unfortunately, due to limited funding, many schools struggle to provide these services adequately. In some cases, students are placed in overcrowded classrooms or have to wait for long periods before receiving the necessary support. This lack of sufficient funding can hinder their academic progress and social development, leading to long-term negative consequences.
Moreover, underfunded special education programs can lead to increased stress on teachers. Special education teachers are already tasked with meeting the unique needs of their students while also managing a variety of behavioral, emotional, and educational challenges. Without sufficient resources, it becomes increasingly difficult for teachers to provide the individualized attention and care that special education students need. This can lead to teacher burnout, high turnover rates, and, ultimately, a decrease in the quality of education provided.
The Importance of Increasing Special Education Funding
Increasing funding for special education is essential for addressing these challenges. By providing adequate financial resources, schools can ensure that special education students receive the support they need to succeed academically and socially. This includes providing smaller class sizes, hiring specialized staff such as speech therapists or occupational therapists, and offering assistive technologies that can help students with physical or learning disabilities engage with the curriculum.
Additionally, more funding would allow for greater professional development opportunities for teachers and staff who work with special education students. Teachers would be better equipped with the tools and training they need to meet the diverse needs of their students, leading to improved educational outcomes. This investment in teacher development can also reduce burnout and increase retention, ensuring a stable and consistent learning environment for students.
Promoting Inclusion and Equal Opportunities
One of the most compelling reasons for increasing special education funding is to promote greater inclusion within the education system. Every student, regardless of their disability, deserves access to a high-quality education. Inadequate funding often results in students being segregated into separate classrooms or even sent to specialized institutions, rather than being integrated into general education settings. This can limit their opportunities to interact with their peers and participate in

extracurricular activities, which are essential for their social and emotional growth.
Increased funding can make it possible for schools to provide inclusive environments where students with disabilities learn alongside their typically developing peers. Research has shown that inclusive education benefits all students, not just those with disabilities. When students with different abilities work together, they develop empathy, communication skills, and an understanding of diversity. By investing in special education, we can foster a more inclusive, compassionate, and equitable society.
The Long-Term Benefits of Increased Special Education Funding
The benefits of increased funding for special education extend beyond the classroom. Students who receive appropriate support and services are more likely to graduate from high school, attend college, and enter the workforce. By giving students with disabilities the tools they need to succeed, we are setting them up for a more independent and fulfilling life. This not only benefits the individual students but also contributes to society as a whole. When students with disabilities are empowered to reach their full potential, they are more likely to contribute positively to their communities and the economy.
Moreover, the financial investment in special education can lead to long-term cost savings. By providing early intervention and adequate support, schools can help prevent the development of more severe issues that may require more expensive services later on. Early intervention has been shown to be one of the most effective ways to support students with disabilities, leading to better outcomes and reducing the need for costly interventions in the future.
Conclusion
In conclusion, increasing special education funding is essential for providing equitable educational opportunities to students with disabilities. Adequate funding ensures that these students receive the support they need to thrive academically and socially, while also promoting inclusion and reducing the strain on teachers. By investing in special education, we are investing in the future of all students, creating a more inclusive, compassionate, and prosperous society. It is time for policymakers to prioritize special education funding and ensure that every student, regardless of their abilities, has the opportunity to succeed.

Testimony by William Norbert

Neither For Nor Against L.D. 98
An Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine Program
Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
February 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Bill Norbert. I am the Governmental Affairs and Communications Manager
at the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME). I am testifying Neither For Nor Against L.D. 98,
An. Act to Include School Counselors in the Educators for Maine Program.
This bill is a Department initiative and would add school counselor as a
postbaccalaureate certification pursuit that is eligible for financial assistance-~a loan and/or loan
forgiveness-~under the Educators for Maine Program, which is administered by FAME.
The Educators for Maine Program provides merit-based forgivable loans for Maine
students pursuing initial certification as a teacher, including speech pathology or a career in child
development. Students may be enrolling in or pursuing undergraduate or graduate education
degrees, but they must demonstrate an interest in careers in education or childcare and that they
are planning to work in Maine after graduation. Award amounts are based on available funding
and are subject to change annually, but not less than $3,000 for undergraduate students and not less than $2,000 for graduate students. For academic year 23-24, awards were $5,000/year for
undergraduates and $4,000/year for graduate studies. Loans may be forgiven if the recipient
subsequently works as an educator or speech pathologist in an eligible elementary or secondary
school or at a quality childcare program in the state of Maine. Loan recipients who are Jobs for Maine's Graduates Specialists may also be eligible for forgiveness in this program.
We have no objection to including school counselors in the Program. Please keep in
mind, however, that without additional funding to accompany this added profession, school counselors will need to compete with other program applicants (graduating high school seniors, college undergraduates, and students pursuing post-baccalaureate certification) for limited
spaces. We anticipate selecting twenty-five individuals in May for the program.
l

We have a couple of suggestions to improve the bill. First, we suggest adding a definition
of "school counselor" in Section l250l-A (Definitions) of the governing program statute to be
clear who we mean precisely. Our understanding from the Department is that they wish to use
the definition currently set forth in statute at 20-A MRS �4008(l)(B), and we have no issue with
that:
a person who is employed as a school counselor in a school setting and who:
(1) Is certified as a school counselor by the department; or
(2) Possesses a minimum of a master's degree in an ap_proved program in guidance and
counseling.
Second, we wish to point out an area in the bill needing clarification. In line 38 of the bill (Page 1), the draft proposes replacing the word "teaches" with "work" in statute. This is understandable
since proponents wish to allow for school counselors to be covered by the program's loan
repayment terms, and they will "work" and not "teach." From our viewpoint, however, considering the teachers who are included in the program already or may apply in the future, changing the term "teaches" to "works" might unintentionally open the program to former teachers who now work at a school but are serving there in an occupation other than teaching
(e. g. ed techs or administrators). We therefore suggest using the following language instead in
that sentence after the words "as long as the recipient" in lines 37-38: "is employed in a certified instructional or student support role, specifically as a teacher" , school counselor, or licensed speech pathologist. in a school in an underserved geographic area."
Thank you for your time and consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you might have.
